column2: On the authority of al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “No human being fills a vessel worse than a stomach.

It is enough for the son of Ādam to have a few mouthfuls to keep his back upright. But if he must, then a third for his food, a third for his drink and a third for his breath.” Reported by Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah; al-Tirmidhī said: “A ḥasan hadith.”
His words ﷺ, “No human being fills a vessel worse than a stomach”: a vessel is a container in which something is placed, and the worst vessel to be filled is the stomach,
because of the indigestion it brings and its causing illness, and because of the laziness, lethargy and inclination to ease it produces.

His words, “It is enough for the son of Ādam to have a few mouthfuls (akalāt) to keep his back upright”, mean that a few mouthfuls that sustain his life are enough for the son of Ādam; this is the meaning of “to keep his ṣulb upright”, ṣulb meaning the back. This urges eating little and not indulging in food,
so that a person enjoys lightness, vigour and safety from the illnesses and ailments that result from eating much.

His words, “But if he must, then a third for his food, a third for his drink and a third for his breath”, mean: if a person is not content with mouthfuls that keep his back upright and must go beyond that amount, then let the amount eaten and drunk be within two thirds of the stomach,
so that a third remains with which one can breathe easily.
The hadith shows the etiquette of the Sharīʿah that the eater should observe in how much he eats.
Filling the stomach is warned against,
because of the illness, laziness and lethargy it brings.
Sufficiency is attained by what sustains life.
If one must eat more than suffices, let it be within two thirds of the stomach.
